degraded.credentials: The cluster refused the credential. Check the username, password and SASL mechanism: a broker that rejects authentication may close the connection instead of explaining, so a wrong mechanism looks the same as a wrong password.
degraded.forbidden: The credential was accepted but is not allowed to describe the cluster. That is fixed with an ACL on the broker, not in this form.
degraded.timeout: The cluster accepted the connection and did not answer in time.
degraded.unreachable: Nothing usable answered at this address. Check the bootstrap servers, and whether the listener expects TLS or a security protocol this connection is not using.
degraded.accessControl: This cluster runs without an authorizer, so it enforces no ACLs and every access-control call answers SECURITY_DISABLED.

form.amqpUrlHint: Left empty, the management host is reused on port 5672 (5671 with TLS).

caveat.browseAltersQueue: Browsing alters the queue: messages are requeued but come back flagged redelivered, and concurrent consumers see the gap.

degraded.managementPlugin: The management API answered 404: nothing is mounted at that address. Check that the management plugin is enabled and that the address points at the management port.
degraded.credentials: The username or password was rejected (the management API answered 401). Check the credentials in the connection settings.
degraded.forbidden: The credentials are valid, but this user has no management tag and cannot read the management API (403). Give it the management tag or higher.
degraded.timeout: Timed out reaching the management API. Check the broker is reachable, or raise the timeout in the connection settings.
degraded.unreachable: Cannot reach the management API. Check the address and port, and that the management plugin is enabled - with it off nothing listens on the management port at all, which looks the same from here as a wrong address.
degraded.amqpAccessRefused: The management API works but the AMQP connection was refused: this user has no permission on the virtual host. Browsing and publishing are unavailable; the admin views are not affected.
degraded.amqpTimeout: Timed out reaching the AMQP port. Check the address and port, and that nothing is filtering it.
degraded.amqpUnreachable: Cannot reach the AMQP port. The admin views still work, but browsing and publishing do not - check the AMQP address and port.
degraded.replicationPlugin: The shovel and federation plugins are not enabled on this broker, so the cross-broker pages have nothing to read. That is a deployment choice rather than a failure - enable them with rabbitmq-plugins enable rabbitmq_shovel rabbitmq_shovel_management.
degraded.streamPlugin: The broker does not have the rabbitmq_stream_management plugin enabled. A stream queue still works over AMQP; only its stream protocol clients are invisible.

rabbitmq.title: Users & permissions
rabbitmq.subtitle: Tags decide what the management API allows; permissions decide what AMQP connections may touch. They are two systems.
rabbitmq.nameFixed: The username is the identity and cannot change
rabbitmq.tagsHint: Only these four mean anything to the broker, and they gate the management API only - not what AMQP may touch
rabbitmq.passwordRequired: Set a password, or say explicitly that this user has none
rabbitmq.passwordNone: None - cannot authenticate with a password
rabbitmq.passwordEditHint: Empty leaves the stored password alone; anything else resets it
rabbitmq.withoutPasswordHint: Creates a user that cannot authenticate with a password. For certificate or OAuth authentication.
rabbitmq.noPermissionsWarn: This user has no permission record on any virtual host, so the broker refuses its connections outright - which looks like a wrong password from the application's side.
rabbitmq.patternHint: All three are regular expressions matched against resource names. Empty permits nothing; .* permits everything. There is no third state.
rabbitmq.configureHint: Declaring and deleting queues and exchanges
rabbitmq.writeHint: Publishing to an exchange, and binding
rabbitmq.readHint: Consuming from a queue, and binding
rabbitmq.revokeDesc: Removes the permission record itself, after which the broker refuses this user's connections to that virtual host outright. That is different from setting all three patterns empty, which lets it connect and then do nothing.
rabbitmq.topicHint: Narrows the permissions above further, on topic exchanges only. It cannot grant what the permissions above do not.
rabbitmq.deleteDesc: Its permissions go with it and the broker closes any connection it currently holds. There is no undo.

kafka.title: Access control
kafka.subtitle: The rules the cluster enforces, and the users it stores
kafka.principalHint: a type and a name, such as User:alice
kafka.noRules: This cluster enforces no rules yet. With an authorizer on and no rule matching, access is refused.
kafka.noUsers: This cluster stores no SCRAM users. A cluster that authenticates over mTLS or Kerberos has principals it never stores, and they still appear in the rules.
kafka.noAuthorizer: This cluster runs without an authorizer, so it enforces no ACLs and every access-control call answers SECURITY_DISABLED. Nothing is wrong with the connection; there is nothing here to show.
kafka.deleteRuleBody: All of this principal's grants go at once. With an authorizer on and no rule matching, its access is refused from that moment.
kafka.deleteUserBody: The user's password is removed for every mechanism it has. Anything authenticating as it stops being able to connect.
kafka.mechanismHint: the two are separate credentials on the broker
kafka.passwordNote: Kafka stores a password salted and cannot be asked for it again, so there is no keeping the old one: saving replaces it.
kafka.prefixedHint: covers every name starting with it
kafka.denyNote: A Deny beats an Allow: if any rule denies an action, it is denied however many rules allow it.

invalid.subjectShape: A principal is a type and a name, such as User:alice
invalid.prefixEmpty: A prefix of nothing matches every resource
invalid.nameColon: A user name cannot contain a colon

rabbitmq.noQueues: No queues in this virtual host yet
rabbitmq.noExchanges: No exchanges in this virtual host
rabbitmq.noBindings: Nothing is bound to this exchange; what is published to it is dropped
rabbitmq.defaultExchangeNote: The default exchange's bindings are implicit: every queue is bound to it by its own name, and the broker lists none of them.
rabbitmq.nameReserved: The amq. prefix is reserved by the broker
rabbitmq.nameHint: Created in virtual host {{vhost}}. A queue's type and arguments are fixed once declared.
rabbitmq.autoDelete: Delete when the last consumer leaves
rabbitmq.autoDeleteHint: For temporary queues. A queue that never had a consumer is not deleted.
rabbitmq.dlxHint: Where messages go when they are rejected, expire, or the queue is full
rabbitmq.dlxRoutingKeyHint: Left empty the message keeps its own routing key, which changes where it lands
rabbitmq.dlxRoutingKeyNeedsExchange: A dead-letter routing key needs a dead-letter exchange
rabbitmq.messageTtlHint: Milliseconds. A message not consumed in that time is dropped or dead-lettered.
rabbitmq.expiresHint: Milliseconds. The queue deletes itself after that long with no consumer and no use.
rabbitmq.overflowHint: What a full queue does: drop the oldest, refuse new ones, or refuse and dead-letter
rabbitmq.singleActiveHint: Only one consumer receives at a time and the rest wait. For strict ordering.

typeHint.quorum: Replicated across nodes; survives losing one. The default choice.
typeHint.classic: Lives on a single node and is lost with it.
typeHint.stream: An append-only log read by offset; consuming does not remove a message.

rabbitmq.deleteHolding: It still holds {{count}} messages. They go with it, and there is no undo.
rabbitmq.deleteEmpty: The queue is empty. There is no undo.
rabbitmq.purgeDesc: Discards the {{count}} messages it holds. The queue itself stays. There is no undo.
rabbitmq.moveWarn: Each message is published to the target and confirmed by the broker before the original is acknowledged, so a failure partway leaves a duplicate rather than a hole. A target nothing is bound to refuses the batch and the source is left alone.
rabbitmq.moveRoutingKeyHint: Left empty each message keeps its own key, which sends the batch back through the topology it originally took
rabbitmq.moveToSelf: The target cannot be the queue itself
rabbitmq.moveLimitHint: One round trip and one confirm per message, so this moves a batch rather than a whole backlog
rabbitmq.rebalanceDesc: Spreads quorum queue leaders back across the nodes. They pile up on whichever node was available when each queue was declared, especially after a rolling restart, and the broker does not spread them on its own.
rabbitmq.exchangeNameHint: Created in virtual host {{vhost}}. An exchange's type is fixed once declared.

exchangeTypeHint.topic: Matches routing key patterns; * is one word, # is any number
exchangeTypeHint.direct: Delivers only on an exact routing key match
exchangeTypeHint.fanout: Ignores the routing key and delivers to everything bound
exchangeTypeHint.headers: Ignores the routing key and matches on headers

rabbitmq.alternateHint: Unroutable messages go here instead of being dropped
rabbitmq.alternateIsSelf: An exchange cannot be its own alternate
rabbitmq.transientHint: The exchange and its bindings disappear when the node restarts
rabbitmq.autoDeleteExchange: Delete when the last binding is removed
rabbitmq.deleteExchangeDesc: Its {{count}} bindings go with it, and anything still publishing to it starts getting errors. There is no undo.
rabbitmq.bindDirectNeedsKey: A direct exchange needs a routing key, or it matches only messages published without one
rabbitmq.bindHeadersNeedsHeaders: A headers exchange needs at least one header to match on

bindKeyHint.topic: Wildcards: * is one word, # is any number of them
bindKeyHint.direct: Must equal the message's routing key exactly
bindKeyHint.fanout: A fanout ignores the routing key; anything here has no effect
bindKeyHint.headers: A headers exchange ignores the routing key

rabbitmq.matchAny: any - one matching header is enough
rabbitmq.unbindDesc: The binding from {{source}} to {{destination}} goes, and nothing is delivered that way afterwards.
rabbitmq.noStreamClients: Nothing is attached over the stream protocol. A stream is readable over AMQP too, and those consumers are counted in the consumer number above.
rabbitmq.noStreamReference: none, so a reconnect is not deduplicated

kafka.subtitle: Topics the cluster holds, internal ones hidden
kafka.settingsNote: As the broker reports them. A value the broker withholds - a password, for instance - is absent rather than blank.
kafka.empty: This cluster has no topics yet. Internal topics are hidden; turn them on to see what the cluster keeps for itself.
kafka.name: Name
kafka.partitionsWarning: Partitions can be added later but never removed.
kafka.deleteBody: Every record in the topic goes with it. Consumer groups reading it lose their committed offsets. This cannot be undone.
kafka.truncateBody: Every record currently in the topic becomes unreadable and the broker reclaims the space on its own schedule. The offsets do not restart: a consumer sitting at 900 stays at 900 and is simply caught up. This cannot be undone.
kafka.rebalanceBody: Each partition's leadership moves back to the first broker in its replica list, which is where Kafka put it when the topic was created. Nothing is copied and no data moves; leadership changes, which briefly interrupts producers on the partitions that move.
kafka.reassignNote: The cluster copies the whole partition to its new brokers in the background, at whatever rate its throttles allow. There is no completion event: the move is done when the partition stops reporting one.

rabbitmq.title: Connections & channels
rabbitmq.subtitle: {{connections}} connections, {{channels}} channels
rabbitmq.search: Search client name, address or user…
rabbitmq.none: No client is connected to this virtual host
rabbitmq.heartbeatOff: Off - neither end notices a dropped network
rabbitmq.noChannels: No channels open on this connection
rabbitmq.closeDesc: Its {{count}} channels close with it and unacknowledged messages are requeued. Most clients reconnect at once - unless whatever reconnects has also been stopped, this only makes it start over.
rabbitmq.closeUserDesc: Every connection this user currently holds is closed. An application usually opens one per instance, and closing them one at a time races the ones reconnecting behind it.
rabbitmq.noChannelClose: RabbitMQ has no endpoint to close a single channel; only whole connections

kafka.subtitle: Groups the cluster holds committed offsets for
kafka.noMembers: Nothing is connected to this group. Its offsets are still here, so it is either between deployments or a consumer that stopped.
kafka.empty: No consumer group has committed an offset on this cluster yet. A group appears the moment one does.
kafka.resetNeedsStop: Kafka will not write a group's offsets while its consumers hold the partitions. Stop them first, then reset.
kafka.timestampHint: the first record at or after it
kafka.clampNote: An offset outside the log lands on its nearest end.
kafka.deleteBody: The group and every offset it has committed go with it. A consumer that reconnects starts wherever its own auto.offset.reset says, which is usually the end.

invalid.timestampInvalid: That is not a valid moment
invalid.shiftZero: A shift of zero changes nothing

rocketmq.noGroups: This cluster has no consumer groups
rocketmq.clientsUnknownHint: The broker did not return this group's connection info, so whether anything is consuming is unknown.
rocketmq.clientSilent: This client did not report the queues it holds
rocketmq.deleteDesc: This removes “{{name}}” and its offsets from every master and cannot be undone. Its retry and dead-letter queues are left in place.

reset.topicPlaceholder: No client is connected, so enter the topic
reset.timeInvalid: That is not a valid time
reset.note: RocketMQ resets by time, not by offset: the broker finds the first message stored at or after that moment, per queue. “Earliest” is the oldest message still retained — anything older has rolled off the commit log.
reset.risky: This moves the read position and can replay or skip messages

clone.title: Clone consume offsets
clone.fromOffline: Read stored offsets (source group is shut down)
clone.risky: Overwrites the target group's current positions
clone.note: Writes the target group the source's exact per-queue offsets, so a replacement group does not replay what the old one handled. Unlike a reset, which finds a position by time, this copies positions.

queueOffset.title: Set the queue's consume offset
queueOffset.note: Unlike a reset, which finds a position by time and moves the whole group, this writes a number to one queue. Past the latest skips what has not arrived; before the earliest is pulled forward by the broker on its next fetch.

form.nameInvalid: A group name cannot contain spaces or %
form.broadcastNote: This sets the broadcast permission the broker stores, not the mode in the list - that is what a connected client reports, and an idle group has none. Saving rewrites the whole subscription config, so untouched fields are written back as they stand.

redis.subtitle: orders:events · 3 groups · PEL 37
redis.bulkHint: Tick rows to act on them together
redis.idleHint: Entries idle over 2h are worth claiming or acknowledging

kafka.subtitle: A range of a log, read forward
kafka.keyScanNote: Kafka indexes nothing but the offset, so a key search reads the log until it finds one. On a busy topic a search that comes back empty has usually run out of budget rather than proved the key is absent.
kafka.dropped: {{count}} records aged out of the log before this tail reached them.
kafka.tailWaiting: Following the end of the log. Records that arrive from now on appear here; what is already stored is the read panel's job.
kafka.tombstone: A key and no value: this is a tombstone, which tells a compacted topic to forget that key.

pulsar.peekNote: Peek does not move the subscription cursor · markDeletePosition 812:2:0

rabbitmq.title: Messages
rabbitmq.subtitle: Take a batch from the head of a queue, look at it, put it back
rabbitmq.ackWarn: Browsing alters the queue: what is taken is put back with nack in its original position, but it comes back flagged redelivered and a concurrent consumer sees the gap while it is out. AMQP has no truly read-only browse of an ordinary queue.
rabbitmq.pickAQueue: Pick a queue, then take a batch
rabbitmq.nothingMatched: Nothing came back - the queue is empty, or nothing matched the filters
rabbitmq.transientWarn: transient - lost on a node restart

replay.noClients: No consumer group has a client connected. This runs on a live instance, so start a consumer first.
replay.note: Runs this client's own handler on the message again and brings back what it returned — for working out why one message in particular fails. It consumes for real: on a client with auto-commit the offset moves.

tail.waitingHint: A live tail starts from the moment it is switched on; what is already stored is what the query above is for.

rocketmq.bodyTruncated: Body too large — showing the first {{shown}} KB of {{total}} KB. The cut-off is a setting.

resend.desc: Puts this message back on the group's retry path for {{topic}}, for whichever member picks it up.

rocketmq.risky: High-risk · written to the audit log
rocketmq.confirmBody: They are rewritten under a new MsgId to {{topic}} for {{group}} to consume normally; the originals stay in the dead-letter queue and can be deleted later.

rabbitmq.title: Dead letters
rabbitmq.subtitle: {{count}} queues are receiving dead letters
rabbitmq.browseWarn: Reading a dead-letter queue is the same browse as any other: messages are taken and put back, and come back flagged redelivered.
rabbitmq.none: No queue in this virtual host declares a dead-letter exchange
rabbitmq.pressFetch: Take a batch to see what is in it

rabbitmq.dropDesc: Takes up to {{count}} from the head and acknowledges them. Acknowledging removes them from the broker with no dead-lettering and no copy anywhere. There is no undo.

producer.noteConfirm: Confirm mode returns ack/nack · mandatory returns anything it cannot route

producer.noSends: Nothing sent in this session yet

rabbitmq.title: Publish
rabbitmq.subtitle: Send to an exchange or straight to a queue, and wait for the broker

addressingHint.queue: Through the default exchange with the queue's name as the routing key - which is what publishing to a queue means in AMQP
addressingHint.exchange: To a named exchange, which decides from the routing key which queues receive it

rabbitmq.persistentHint: Off, the message lives in memory only and is lost when the node restarts - even on a durable queue
rabbitmq.mandatoryHint: Off, a message no queue receives is dropped by the broker and still confirmed, so this console would report the loss as a success
rabbitmq.countHint: Sends the same message repeatedly, for load or for filling a queue. Each waits for its own confirm.
rabbitmq.headersHint: One per line, as kind=order. A headers exchange matches on exactly these.
rabbitmq.expirationHint: Milliseconds. A per-message TTL, after which it is dropped or dead-lettered.
rabbitmq.priorityHint: Only honoured on a queue declared with x-max-priority; ignored otherwise

kafka.title: Send
kafka.subtitle: Write one record, or many, and be told where it landed
kafka.acksNoneWarning: With acks=none the cluster is never asked, so a reported success is not evidence the record was kept and there are no coordinates to read it back by.
kafka.keyHint: off sends a record with no key at all, which Kafka spreads across partitions

invalid.partitionInvalid: A partition is a whole number, or blank to let the key decide
invalid.headerLine: Each header is one key=value per line

nav.title: Navigation model
nav.subtitle: Three layers and where they are isolated: window → connection tab → page. Tabs share no state; drag one out for a new window, or set two side by side to compare.
nav.windowA: Window A (more than one can be open)
nav.pageLayer: Page layer: each tab keeps its own sidebar position, filters, scroll and query results
nav.tearOff: Drag a tab out → window B
nav.sideBySide: Two tabs side by side → split compare
nav.sideBySideNote: Check backlog and messages on both sides during a migration or dual write
nav.isolation: Isolated: page state · query cache · refresh timers · credential sessions · alert subscriptions. Shared: settings · the connection library · the notification centre.

state.offlineHint: This tab's connection is not open. Connect it from the connection list and this page will start reading.

rabbitmq.title: Virtual hosts
rabbitmq.subtitle: {{count}} of them - queues, exchanges, bindings, policies and permissions all live inside one and none is visible from another
rabbitmq.none: No virtual hosts could be read
rabbitmq.name: Name
rabbitmq.nameHint: Cannot be renamed afterwards - a rename is a new virtual host
rabbitmq.nameFixed: The name is the identity and cannot change
rabbitmq.defaultQueueTypeHint: What a queue declared here without a type becomes. Most client libraries declare without one, so whatever is chosen here is what most queues will be.
rabbitmq.tagsHint: Comma separated, for people; the broker does nothing with them
rabbitmq.tracingHint: Copies every message through this virtual host to a log exchange. It is expensive and is meant for minutes of diagnosis, not to be left on.
rabbitmq.limitHint: Empty means no limit - which is not the same as 0, and 0 allows none at all
rabbitmq.deleteDesc: Its queues, {{count}} messages, exchanges, bindings, policies and permissions go with it. There is no undo.
rabbitmq.deleteFailed: Could not delete the virtual host

rabbitmq.title: Policies
rabbitmq.subtitle: A queue's arguments are fixed once declared; a policy is the only way to change a running one
rabbitmq.name: Name
rabbitmq.nameFixed: The name is the identity; a rename is a new policy
rabbitmq.patternHint: A regular expression matched against queue or exchange names. ^order\\. matches everything starting with order.
rabbitmq.applyToHint: A definition meant for quorum queues applied to all queues is rejected on every classic queue it matches, and the broker reports that per queue rather than when the policy is saved
rabbitmq.priorityHint: Only one policy applies to a given queue - the highest-priority match. Policies do not merge.
rabbitmq.priorityNote: Only the highest-priority matching policy applies. The others have no effect at all; they are not merged.
rabbitmq.operatorHint: Operator policies are set by whoever runs the broker; where both set the same key, the more restrictive value wins
rabbitmq.definitionInvalid: The definition is not valid JSON
rabbitmq.definitionNotObject: The definition must be a JSON object
rabbitmq.definitionEmpty: The definition is empty - this policy would match queues and change nothing about them
rabbitmq.deleteDesc: Every queue matched by {{pattern}} reverts to whatever it was declared with, immediately and with no warning from the broker.
rabbitmq.parameterHint: Configuration the broker stores for its plugins. Shovels and federation upstreams live here - read and delete only, because a parameter's shape belongs to whichever plugin owns it and nothing here can validate one.
rabbitmq.deleteParameterDesc: It belongs to the {{component}} component, whose configuration it is.

rabbitmq.title: Definitions
rabbitmq.subtitle: The whole topology as one JSON document - RabbitMQ's only backup of anything but messages
rabbitmq.brokerScopeHint: Includes every user and permission, and every user's password hash - treat the file as a credential
rabbitmq.vhostScopeHint: Only this virtual host's queues, exchanges, bindings, policies and parameters. No users or permissions: those are broker-wide.
rabbitmq.exportHint: Written as a JSON file. It is what a cluster is rebuilt from.
rabbitmq.importHint: Choose a file, see what is in it, then decide whether to apply it.
rabbitmq.empty: There is nothing in this file
rabbitmq.additiveWarn: Importing adds and overwrites; it does not synchronise. Anything named in the document is created or overwritten, and anything on the broker the document does not mention is left exactly as it is - so this cannot make a cluster match a file, only put the file's contents into it.
rabbitmq.importDesc: Creates or overwrites {{count}} objects. A queue, exchange, policy or user of the same name is replaced by the file's version, and there is no undo.

rabbitmq.title: Replication
rabbitmq.subtitle: Shovels and federation - the two ways messages move between brokers
rabbitmq.shovelHint: A shovel moves messages from somewhere to somewhere and is done. Its definition carries the other broker's credentials in a URI, so these are read and delete only - one is declared where the rest of a deployment is.
rabbitmq.federationHint: Federation keeps two brokers' exchanges or queues in step continuously. An upstream is configuration; the link is the connection.
rabbitmq.redacted: The password was removed before this left the broker
rabbitmq.deleteShovelDesc: It stops moving messages at once. Anything not yet moved stays in the source queue; nothing is lost.
rabbitmq.deleteUpstreamDesc: Its links close and the two brokers stop keeping each other in step.

kafka.title: Quotas
kafka.subtitle: What the cluster will let one client do, in total
kafka.name: Name
kafka.isDefaultHint: every client of this type with no quota of its own
kafka.deleteBody: Every limit on this entity is cleared. Clients it covered fall back to the default for their type, or to no limit at all if there is none.
kafka.zeroNote: A blank field leaves a limit alone. A zero is a real quota that throttles the client to nothing, so it is not the way to say “no limit”.
kafka.empty: This cluster enforces no client quotas. Every client can use as much of it as it asks for.

invalid.entityRequired: Pick what the quota applies to
invalid.nameRequired: Enter a name, or make it the default
invalid.duplicateType: Each dimension can only appear once
invalid.ipCombination: An IP quota throttles connections before anyone authenticates, so it cannot be combined with a user or client id
invalid.limitInvalid: A limit is a number and cannot be negative
